title: 6 errand businesses to start under $40
description: Six legit errand businesses you can start for under $40, with checked starter gear prices, what customers pay pros, and how to land your first 3 clients.
image_alt: Infographic: 6 errand businesses to start under $40: package pickup ~$40, grocery runs ~$15, gift shopping free, return runs ~$13, line sitting ~$11, plant watering ~$5.
intro: Busy weeks, and especially the holidays, leave a lot of people short on time for the small jobs: mailing packages, picking up groceries, returning things, standing in line. Each idea below starts with one inexpensive item and the car or transit pass you already use. The most expensive one is package pickup, at about $40 for a folding cart that holds 90 lb. The cheapest, gift shopping, is free to start with a free Google Voice number.

Below are the six ideas from our post, with the exact product we priced on a real store page, what customers typically pay for the same errand where a reliable price guide exists, and the simplest way to land your first three clients. Start with people you know, be on time, keep every receipt, and let happy clients send their friends your way.

ideas.name: Package Pickup
ideas.first_job: Taking a neighbor's holiday packages to the post office
ideas.what: You collect packages from clients' homes or offices and take them to the post office or a shipping store, or pick up deliveries held at a pickup point. It's especially handy in November and December, when people are mailing gifts and lines are long.
ideas.who: you have a reliable car or live close to a post office, are organized, and are happy to lift and carry boxes.

kit.item: DMI compact folding shopping cart (holds 90 lb)

ideas.kit_note: Take a photo of each package and keep the shipping receipt for the client. Lift with your legs, and split heavy loads into more than one trip.

charge.text: Taskrabbit's errand cost guide puts **mailing packages at $20 to $45** per errand. Errand running overall averages **$28 per hour** in the U.S., and most states average **between $25.00 and $35.50 per hour**.

first_customers: Post in your neighborhood Facebook group or Nextdoor in early November offering holiday package drop-offs, with a simple flat price per trip.
Ask small home businesses you know (Etsy sellers, bakers, crafters) if they'd like a regular weekly post office run.
Leave a short flyer with older neighbors or at a senior center, if allowed, and ask happy clients to pass your number along.
ideas.watch_out: never accept a package if you don't know what's inside, and don't ship anything the carrier doesn't allow. Agree in writing who pays postage and how, and hand over every receipt and tracking number the same day.

ideas.name: Grocery Runs
ideas.first_job: A weekly grocery run for a busy parent or an older neighbor
ideas.what: You shop from a client's list, or pick up an order they've already placed, and bring it to their door. Regular weekly clients are the goal: same day, same store, same routine.
ideas.who: you're careful with lists, notice details like ripe produce and expiration dates, and like a steady routine.
ideas.kit_note: Shop cold and frozen items last, keep them in the insulated bags, and go straight to the client's home after checkout.

charge.text: Taskrabbit's errand cost guide puts **grocery pickup at $20 to $50** and **grocery shopping at $30 to $60** per errand. The cost of the groceries themselves is added on top.

first_customers: Offer one free or discounted grocery run to a family member or neighbor in exchange for an honest review.
Ask at your place of worship, a local parents' group or a senior community whether anyone needs a regular weekly shopper.
Offer a set weekly time slot so clients can count on you, and ask each happy client for one referral.
ideas.watch_out: agree in advance how you'll be paid back for groceries, and give the client the receipt every time. Keep a short substitution plan for out-of-stock items, and keep cold food cold. Don't buy alcohol or medicine for a client unless you know your state's rules allow it.

ideas.name: Gift Shopping
ideas.first_job: Holiday gifts for a busy coworker's family
ideas.what: You shop for gifts for clients who don't have the time: holiday lists, birthdays, teacher and coworker gifts, or thank-you gifts for a small business. Many clients also like you to wrap and deliver them.
ideas.who: you enjoy shopping, are good at finding the right thing on a budget, and stay organized with lots of names and sizes.

kit.item: Google Voice number for client calls and texts

ideas.kit_note: A separate number keeps your personal phone private. Google says its no-charge plan is for personal, consumer use and is only available in the US; it needs a personal Gmail account and a phone number to forward calls to.

charge.text: There's no separate national price guide for gift-shopping errands, so most errand runners charge their usual hourly rate. Taskrabbit's errand cost guide puts errand running at **$28 per hour** on average in the U.S., with the cost of the items bought added to the bill.

first_customers: Offer a holiday gift-shopping package to coworkers or friends with long lists, with a clear hourly price and an agreed budget per gift.
Ask local small business owners if they'd like help buying and delivering client or employee thank-you gifts.
Share photos of nicely wrapped gifts (with permission, no names) in your neighborhood group to show your work.
ideas.watch_out: agree on the budget for each gift in writing before you shop, and never go over it without asking. Keep every receipt and gift receipt, and don't use your own credit card for large purchases unless you're sure you'll be paid back right away.

ideas.name: Return Runs
ideas.first_job: Returning a neighbor's online orders after the holidays
ideas.what: You take clients' unwanted purchases back to the store, or pack up online returns and drop them at a shipping location. It's busiest right after the holidays and after big sales.
ideas.who: you're patient in customer service lines and careful about paperwork and receipts.

kit.item: Scotch heavy duty packaging tape with dispenser

ideas.kit_note: Photograph each item and its return label before you seal the box, and keep the drop-off receipt for the client.

charge.text: Taskrabbit's errand cost guide puts **store returns at $20 to $40** per errand.

first_customers: Post a simple "holiday returns" offer in your neighborhood group for the last week of December and early January.
Offer to bundle returns for several neighbors on the same street into one trip, at a lower price each.
Ask happy clients to keep your number for the next big sale season.
ideas.watch_out: store refunds usually go back to the original card, so the client stays in control of the money. Check each store's return window and rules before you go, and only return items with the client's receipt or order number.

ideas.name: Line Sitting
ideas.first_job: Holding a spot in line for a local holiday event or a restaurant opening
ideas.what: You wait in line so your client doesn't have to: for a popular product release, a restaurant opening, a free community event or a busy office. When the line gets close, the client takes your place or you complete the errand for them.
ideas.who: you're patient, don't mind early mornings, and can stay comfortable and polite for hours.
ideas.kit_note: Dress for the weather in layers, bring a charged phone and power bank, and keep water and snacks with you.

charge.text: Taskrabbit's errand cost guide puts **waiting in line at $30 to $125**, depending on how long the wait runs.

first_customers: Watch your local news and social pages for big openings, launches and events, and post an offer to hold a spot a few days before.
Offer friends a discounted first line-sit in exchange for a review and a referral.
Charge a clear hourly rate with a minimum, so long waits are fair to you.
ideas.watch_out: some events, venues and government offices don't allow paid line holding or ticket resale, so check the rules first. Never hold a spot where you'd be blocking others unfairly, and don't wait alone in unsafe places or late at night.

ideas.name: Plant Watering
ideas.first_job: Watering a neighbor's plants while they travel for the holidays
ideas.what: You visit clients' homes while they're away and water their indoor plants and patio pots, following their instructions. Many clients also ask you to bring in the mail and check that everything looks fine.
ideas.who: you're trustworthy, reliable with schedules, and live close to the homes you'll visit.
ideas.kit_note: Ask each client for written watering instructions for each plant, and send a quick photo after every visit.
ideas.charge_fallback: We couldn't find a reliable national cost guide for plant-watering visits, and prices vary a lot by area and by how many plants there are. Search local house-sitting and plant-sitting listings, note what they charge per visit, and price yours in that range. Put the visit schedule and price in writing.
first_customers: Tell neighbors you know who travel for the holidays that you can water their plants while they're away.
Post in your neighborhood group or Nextdoor with a simple price per visit and the area you cover.
Ask happy clients to recommend you to friends who travel often.
ideas.watch_out: you'll be trusted with someone's keys and home. Get a written agreement with the visit dates, keep keys labeled with no address, never bring anyone else inside, and tell the client right away if anything looks wrong.

getting_started: **Check local rules.** Search "[your city] business license" to see whether you need one for an errand service. Rules vary by city and state.
**Check your car insurance.** If you drive for these errands, ask your insurer whether your policy covers driving for paid work.
**Put it in writing.** Send a short message with the errand, date, price and how you'll be paid back for any purchases before every job.
**Keep every receipt.** Hand clients their receipts and tracking numbers, and keep copies for yourself.
**Track every dollar.** Side income is taxable, so record what you earn, keep a log of business miles, and set some aside.
tip: Sell **prepaid 5-errand packs** so busy clients book once and you get paid upfront.

faq.q: Which of these is cheapest to start?
faq.a: Gift shopping is free to start with a free Google Voice number. Plant watering starts at about $5 for a 2 gallon watering can, and line sitting at about $11 for a camping stool.

faq.q: Do I need a business license?
faq.a: It depends on your city and state. Many places require a general business license for paid services, even part-time. Check your city's website or call the clerk's office before you start.
We don't promise earnings. Where we show prices, they're what customers typically pay for the same errands, from published cost guides. As a beginner, expect to charge less until you have reviews.
Not for every idea. Line sitting and plant watering can work on foot or by transit if your clients live nearby. Package pickup and grocery runs are much easier with a car.

Plant watering for neighbors and line sitting with a parent's OK can work for teens. Anything involving driving or handling a client's money is better for adults. Check your state's rules for working minors.
